entries.title: US judge orders halt to taxpayer-funded promo ads of Trump
entries.summary: Last week, President Donald Trump said he considered the ads to be a "positive promotion for our great USA." However, the New York district judge ruled that the commercials were an illegal misuse of funds.
entries.content:
United States of America

US judge orders halt to taxpayer-funded promo ads of Trump

October 12, 2026

Last week, President Donald Trump said he considered the ads to be a "positive promotion for our great USA." However, the New York district judge ruled that the commercials were an illegal misuse of funds.

US President Donald Trump must cancel any remaining television ads paid for with millions in taxpayer money for political promotions, a federal court judge ruled on Sunday night, granting a temporary restraining order.

This comes after publicly funded television ads glorifying Trump began airing in late September, sparking bipartisan backlash.

The commercials feature Trump promoting his policies and warning against communism and of a "final battle" against "globalists."

They end with a disclaimer saying they were paid for by the US government.

What did the judge say?

New York District Judge Jennifer L Rochon called the commercials an illegal misuse of funds, siding with a coalition which includes the nonpartisan watchdog Common Cause.

"Defendants shall not enter into, renew, or expand any agreement authorizing the development, creation, dissemination, placement, or airing of the challenged advertisements" during the two-week duration of her order, the judge said.

The court ordered the halt even as the administration said the ad campaign was coming to an end. In a court filing late on Saturday, the Justice Department had argued that the temporary restraining order was unnecessary because "the alleged offending conduct will end tomorrow."

What is the controversy?

The Department of Homeland Security tapped $20 million (€17.8 million) taxpayer funds to run the ads in question.

Legal experts argue that it violates a federal statute against congressionally appropriated money being used for "publicity or propaganda," along with other laws potentially.

On Monday, Trump had said he considered the ads to be "rather standard" and a "positive promotion for our great USA," but that they would not be funded by taxpayers any longer.

The White House said last week that the president's political action committee would fund the ads going forward but not reimburse taxpayers for the ones that had already run on their dime.

"There is no legal justification — and no precedent — for the president to use the machinery of the government and funds set aside by Congress for other uses to influence electoral outcomes that further his own agenda," the plaintiffs said in a statement issued by Democracy Forward, a nonprofit organization that represents them.

"We won't stop until this administration is ‌held fully accountable, and no president from any party can waste ‌and ​abuse taxpayer funds for propaganda ever again," said Common Cause President and CEO Virginia Kase Solomon.

The plaintiffs, which included a public employee union and a candidate for Alabama state representative, urged the judge to block the ads by Friday so they would not air during weekend programming, such as football games and Saturday Night Live.

US Democrats have also challeneged the ads in a seperate suit filed at a federal court in Washington.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: North Korea fires missiles after Seoul's hypersonic test
entries.summary: North Korea has conducted its fourth missile launch in October. South Korea's military called this launch a "show of force" in response to South Korea's successful test launch of a hypersonic missile.
entries.content:
North Korea

North Korea fires missiles after Seoul's hypersonic test

October 12, 2026

North Korea has conducted its fourth missile launch in October. South Korea's military called this launch a "show of force" in response to South Korea's successful test launch of a hypersonic missile.

North Korea fired multiple ballistic missiles into the sea on Monday morning, South Korea's military said.

South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said various types of missiles were fired from the Pyongyang area. One of them flew more than 900 kilometers (559 miles) before falling into the sea.

Japan's coast guard also detected two objects that were fired from North Korea.

'A show of force'

North Korea has conducted numerous missile tests on more than 10 occasions this year, including four in October alone.

Monday's test came after South Korean South Korean President Lee Jae Myung announced the rare test firing of a new hypersonic missile.

South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff called Noth Korea's latest launch "a show of force in response to the successful test launch of our hypersonic missile, as well as an ⁠intentional demonstration ​of missile capabilities."

The missile tests also come amid the backdrop of rising tensions over a North Korean landmine that exploded near the demilitarized zone (DMZ) last month, injuring three South Korean soldiers.

entries.title: Saudi Arabia: Second strike kills at least 1 at Riyadh airport
entries.summary: Sunday's strike came as the King Khalid International Airport remained closed after a deadly attack on Saturday, and after a warning from Houthi rebels in Yemen that "worse is yet to come." Dammam airport was also hit.
entries.content:
Saudi Arabia

Saudi Arabia: Second strike kills 1 at Riyadh airport

Published October 11, 2026last updated October 12, 2026

Sunday's strike came as the King Khalid International Airport remained closed after a deadly attack on Saturday, and after a warning from Houthi rebels in Yemen that "worse is yet to come." Dammam airport was also hit.

At least one person was killed and 11 others were injured in a stike on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Sunday, a day after a similar attack killed 12 and injured hundreds.

"King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh was subjected to a new attack on Sunday afternoon," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement.

It later confirmed that the individual killed in the Sunday attack was a Pakistani national.

A spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition fighting Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said that a cruise missile had been intercepted by air defense systems in the vicinity of the airport, but no further details were immediately available.

The Houthis later claimed responsibility for the strikes, saying they had "carried out four qualitative operations in the past 24 hours using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones."

A spokesman said the group targeted the Riyadh airport multiple times, as well as the Dammam airport in the east of the country and two facilities belonging to the Saudi state oil company Aramco.

Later on Sunday evening, Saudi authorities also confirmed an attack on Dammam airport.

Houthis warn airlines to avoid Saudi Arabia

The latest Houthi strikes also came just hours after the rebel group warned airlines and travelers to avoid Saudi airports.

"We renew our warning to all airlines, experts, employees, workers and travelers against using Saudi airports and airspace, as they are vulnerable to attack and have become a theater of operations for our forces," read a statement released by the group on social media. It added that airports in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina would not be targeted.

"We ‌urge everyone to take our warnings seriously," the statement continued, stating: "Saudi Arabia bears responsibility for any failed interceptions."

Why are Saudi airports being targeted?

Saudi Arabia has stepped up its military involvement in Yemen in recent weeks, launching strikes against the Houthis and backing a Yemeni government counteroffensive after the rebels seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month, including around the vital Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

The Houthi-run health authority claimed this weekend that 91 Yemenis have been killed by the Saudi-led coalition in the last five weeks, 60% of them women and children. Earlier on Sunday, it said a child was killed and six people wounded in a suspected Saudi airstrike on a house in Sanaa.

The Houthi-run Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi Arabia had struck the international airport in Sanaa on Sunday afternoon.

There was no immediate comment from Saudi authorities on the claims.

"Unless the Saudi enemy stops its aggression and interference in Yemen, worse is yet to come, God willing," the Houthi-run Foreign Ministry said in statements carried by Al Masirah TV on Sunday, adding that its ​actions would be guided by the principle of reciprocity.

What has Saudi Arabia said about the Riyadh airport attacks?

The Saudi-led coalition, which supports the internationally recognized Yemeni government in its conflict against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, vowed a tough response to the attack, which it labeled a "full-fledged war crime."

The Houthi strikes on Riyadh come amid a surge in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia this week, which have targeted other airports, military sites and oil infrastructure.

The spike in attacks has followed a major military offensive by the Saudi-led coalition against the Houthis.

The rebels, one of Tehran's regional proxies, have been fighting Yemen's government, which is recognized by the international community, since the outbreak of a civil war over a decade ago.

While a truce in 2022 froze the conflict, it failed to secure a lasting peace deal. The US-Israeli war with Iran has seen fighting flare up again in Yemen, worsening an already severe humanitarian crisis.

How has the international community reacted to the Riyadh strikes?

US President Donald Trump on Saturday said he would be speaking to Saudi Arabia's de facto leader, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, in the wake of the attack, which he said was "not acceptable."

Trump also said that the US was "going to look" at potentially joining Saudi strikes against the rebels.

On Sunday, European leaders expressed their "shock" at the attack on Riyadh airport.

The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said the EU stands in "solidarity with Saudi Arabia" as she condemned the "dangerous escalation."

"These attacks by Iran's proxies are pushing the region into a spiral of violence. They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes with shock waves sent through the world," von der Leyen said.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul "firmly" condemned what he described as "a terrorist act against Saudi Arabia and civil aviation".

"Our thoughts are with the victims and I send my sincere condolences to their loved ones," he said on X.

UK Defense Secretary Wes Streeting slammed the attacks as "contemptible" and a "dangerous escalation," while the French Foreign Ministry condemned the "heinous attack" and stressed its "total solidarity" with Saudi Arabia.

Russia, which is a strategic partner of Iran, also condemned the Houthis' attack and called for the hostilities to end "through political and diplomatic means."

Australia, meanwhile, has urged its citizens in the Saudi capital to "shelter in place" amid the escalating attacks.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru, Wesley Rahn

entries.title: UK's Burnham accuses Russia of meddling in Brexit vote
entries.summary: The UK prime minister called for voters in Europe to be made fully aware of Russia's attempts to influence politics.
entries.content:
United Kingdom

UK's Burnham accuses Russia of meddling in Brexit vote

October 12, 2026

The UK prime minister called for voters in Europe to be made fully aware of Russia's attempts to influence politics.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Sunday became the first British leader to openly complain of Russian tampering in the Brexit referendum a decade ago.

Burnham, who took on the role in July from Keir Starmer, thinks leaving the European Union did "more harm than good" and has opened the door to closer ties, including possibly rejoining the bloc.

What did Burnham say?

Burnham told The Rest Is Politics podcast that he had posed the question upon first arriving in Downing Street, and was given a "clear answer that yes, there was [a link to Russian interference]."

He did not provide evidence of the Kremlin's efforts to influence the June 2016 vote, where the UK decided to leave the EU by a 52% to 48% majority.

With the rise of far-right parties in the UK and across the EU, Burnham ​said voters needed better information about efforts by rogue states to disrupt their democracies.

"These things are important now to put clearly on the ​record, and I believe, ‌help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," he said.

Burnham described how German Chancellor Friedrich Merz had told him during talks in Berlin this week that the AfD is "clearly linked to Russia — funded, I believe.”

"There is certainly misinformation, disinformation that is emanating from Russia into German politics,” Burnham added.

'Leaver' Johnson denied Russian meddling

Burnham's Brexit remarks contrast with former Prime Minister Boris Johnson, who campaigned to leave the EU. In 2020, Johnson said ​there was no evidence of Russian sway.

The UK Parliament’s Intelligence and Security Committee found in 2020 that the government had failed to fully assess how Russian state-run media and “troll” accounts could have impacted the vote.

In its report, the Committee also found the Kremlin sought to influence Scotland's 2014 independence referendum, which was rejected by voters.

The UK's intelligence agencies believe Russia continues to spread disinformation to undermine public trust, alongside cyberattacks, sabotage and espionage. They say the issue is getting worse and is often aided by artificial intelligence (AI).

Russia has long denied meddling in other countries' elections or referendums.

After the Brexit vote, it cast some British politicians as gripped by anti-Russian hysteria.

How have UK attitudes toward Brexit changed?

Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.

Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave. Last month, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.

Last month, Burnham said he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.

EU officials have welcomed the change in tone from London, while France and Spain have spoken positively about closer ties, including rejoining.

Some experts remain skeptical, however. Professor Iain Begg of the London School of Economics thinks rejoining would reopen deep political divisions, be complicated from both the EU and UK sides and likely take years.

Edited by: Dmytro Hubenko

entries.title: Air strikes kill dozens of gold miners on Sudan-Egypt border
entries.summary: A Sudan-based rights group said 72 people were killed in a remote, disputed area known for illegal gold mining.
entries.content:
Africa

Air strikes kill dozens of gold miners on Sudan-Egypt border

October 11, 2026

A Sudan-based rights group said 72 people were killed in a remote, disputed area known for illegal gold mining.

At least 72 workers were killed in air strikes on a disputed border area between Sudan  and Egypt that targeted artisanal gold miners, a human rights group said Sunday.

The attack, south of the remote Halayeb triangle, east of the River Nile, is the second of its kind this year.

It comes amid growing concern in Egypt over large-scale displacement from the three-and-a-half-year conflict in Sudan, which has spurred a cross-border exodus.

What do we know?

The Sudan-based Emergency Lawyers, a human rights and legal advocacy organization, said the attack occurred on Saturday in rugged and mountainous territory that it said lies within Sudan.

The Halayeb triangle, which is claimed by both Egypt and Sudan, is known for mining and the gold trade, along with other illicit goods and human trafficking.

The rights group accused the Egyptian air force of carrying out the strikes.

"The repeated attacks on the gold- and mineral-rich border regions reflect a desire by Egyptian authorities to expand and assert control over Sudan's natural resources," it claimed.

Egypt has yet to comment on the strikes, but has previously admitted conducting a "large-scale operation" against illegal gold mining within its borders.

Independent verification remains difficult because of the remote location.

Death toll expected to rise

Sudan Doctors Network warned on Facebook of an expected increase in the number of casualties "due to the severity of some injuries and the difficulties in accessing medical care and essential services in the region."

One survivor told the AFP news agency there were thousands of people working at the remote site when it was hit.

"After the air strike, people scattered. Some people came to Al-Ansary [gold] market, others went in the other direction. That's why no one knows exactly how many were killed," he said.

Strikes tied to war's gold economy

Sudan's civil war between Abdel Fattah al-Burhan's military junta and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) has killed more than 200,000 people and triggered a severe humanitarian crisis.

Despite backing Sudan's army chief al-Burhan, Egypt considers the war at its border a threat to its security.

The RSF has funded its operations by smuggling thousands of tons of gold from Sudan's Darfur and Kordofan regions. According to the UK-based think tank Chatham House, as much as 60% of unofficial gold exports end up in Egypt.

In June, air strikes on mining sites in the same border area were followed by a large-scale Egyptian security operation.

Hundreds of people, including foreigners, were arrested, accused of illegal gold mining and smuggling.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Who are the Ukrainian 'volunteers' under Russian command?
entries.summary: Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Who are the Ukrainian 'volunteers' under Russian command?

October 11, 2026

Russia has announced a battalion consisting of Ukrainian "volunteers." But veterans and former prisoners of war share very different accounts.

Pavlo Oliynyk, 25, says he joined enemy forces to escape Russian captivity. Before his capture in the Donbas region in 2024, he was a senior lieutenant for Ukraine's armed forces.

As a prisoner of war (POW), he says he was electrocuted, beaten and psychologically tortured. So when he received the offer to join the Maksym Kryvonis battalion — named after a famous 17th-century Cossack commander — he accepted.

Oliynyk says he wanted to use this opportunity to reach the front lines, so he could escape to Ukrainian-controlled territory. DW was able to contact Oliynyk through his lawyer.

'Ukrainian volunteers' consist mostly of POWs

Reports of Russian combat units consisting of Ukrainian prisoners of war and former service members of Ukraine's armed forces began emerging in late 2022. Several detachments were initially formed and in August 2026, they were merged into the so-called "Ukrainian Volunteer Special Forces Brigade."

Of the individual units, the Maksym Kryvonis battalion has perhaps drawn the most public attention for having evidently taken part in combat. Its true size is unknown — Russian media reports claim about 200 fighters while available footage only suggests several dozen.

An investigative team of the Ukrainian public broadcaster Suspilne has identified over 30 members and confirmed they are all former Ukrainian servicemen, captured by Russian forces between 2023 and 2024.

An 'imitation' of Russian legions fighting for Ukraine

Pavel Luzin, an expert for Russian foreign policy and defense at the Center for European Policy Analysis, believes these units are an "imitation" of the Russian Volunteer Corps and the Freedom of Russia Legion — units in the Ukrainian armed forces, consisting of Russian citizens — and an attempt by Moscow to distract from the fact that these units exist in the first place. Ukrainian intelligence services tend to agree.

"It bothers them that Russians would fight on Ukraine's side, but Ukrainians won't fight on Russia's side," Yevhen Shybalov, author and veteran of the war in Ukraine, told DW. He added that Russian troops have never tried to hide the fact that Russian volunteer units in Ukrainian ranks were the main reason Russian forces wanted to create Ukrainian units for their own ranks.

Just how voluntary are these combat units?

In 2025, the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) reported that 95% of the released Ukrainian POWs interviewed reported torture or ill-treatment during Russian captivity.

Bill Wiley, executive director of the NGO Commission for International Justice and Accountability, said the physical and psychological state of the returned combatants raises serious doubts that their recruitment was voluntary. Mykhailo Savva of the Center for Civil Liberties, a Kyiv-based human rights organization, points to the criminal procedures running against several of the battalion members, which he said indicates that these suggest the combatants had switched sides voluntarily.

But where to draw the line between voluntary and involuntary recruitment? The war veteran and human rights activist Maksym Butkevych, who spent 28 months as a prisoner of war, said the conditions in Russian captivity make that line hard to distinguish. On the one hand, he said, there is a constant atmosphere of pressure, and on the other hand, it's not implausible that some prisoners defected out of ideological proximity.

How were Ukrainian prisoners made to join Russian forces?

Butkevych told DW that between 2022 and 2023, all Ukrainian prisoners of war had received offers, "more or less persistently," to join the Russian army. In his case, he recounted, it was after he had been severely mistreated.

"They showed us they could do anything they wanted to us," he explained, "which was why we should agree to everything."

The veteran Shybalov reported similar experiences, speaking of attempts to force confessions of war crimes, or to recruit members for Russia's intelligence services. He told DW all prisoners were first interrogated and then made certain propositions under duress.

"You can torture people to get them to confess, but there comes the difficult moment when you need to give them a weapon," he said. "That's why it's more about psychological pressure, and forcing voluntary compliance."

Butkevych confirmed these accounts with his own tales. But neither veteran has ever met someone willing to join Russian units, they said.

What happens after conscription?

Oliynyk, from the Maksym Kryvonis battalion, said he initially turned down multiple bids to join Russian forces. He said he only accepted the fourth offer so he could flee.

He claimed he didn't sign official Defense Ministry paperwork, but a private contract with an individual offering military services. Afterwards, he said, he was brought to a room where he heard lectures and saw videos and photos he was later asked to retell.

Control and mistreatment

Oliynyk said fellow service members in the Maksym Kryvonis battalion consisted both of those who had switched sides of their own volition, and those who had been forced.

In a video circulating online that appears to be of a trial in Ukraine, he also says former Ukrainian POWs in the unit were followed and guarded by mercenaries of the private Russian military company Redut. In the same video, he also speaks of beatings and torture, and receiving monthly wages in envelopes handed out by a member of Russia's military intelligence.

Oliynyk told DW he had been given a phone, but that he was too scared to call anyone in Ukraine because it was under constant surveillance. He denied having fought against Ukrainians, as he fled in March 2025 before his first deployment in the Donetsk province. After running across a field, he said he spent two days hiding from drones in basements and houses before making contact with Ukrainian fighters.

Now, Oliynyk has been in detention in Ukraine for nearly two years while authorities investigate possible treason. He has yet to be formally charged.

Sergey Nikitin contributed to this article, which originally appeared in Ukrainian.

entries.title: German 'lawfare': When lawsuits become a political weapon
entries.summary: The Left Party is suing two government ministers for accusing them of antisemitism, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz has been sued several times by various parties. Is German politics descending into "lawfare?"
entries.content:
Germany

German 'lawfare': When lawsuits become a political weapon

October 11, 2026

The Left Party is suing two government ministers for accusing them of antisemitism, while Chancellor Friedrich Merz has been sued several times by various parties. Is German politics descending into "lawfare?"

A verbal slip, an attempted quip, a lawsuit: Things can move fast in the rancorous atmosphere that currently rules German politics.

The brief exchange happened on a political TV talk show shortly after the Berlin election on September 20, won by the socialist Left Party. The show's host, Maybrit Illner, quickly corrected herself after accidentally saying of the Left Party's Berlin mayoral candidate, "Elif Eralp says she is an antisemite…. She is not an antisemite."

One of her guests, Federal Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, of the conservative Christian Social Union (CSU), responded immediately: "Na doch" (or, "well, yes she is"). In the angry fallout, the Left Party's lawyers jumped on these two words, and have filed a lawsuit, arguing that this amounted to defamation of Eralp, as it falsely suggested that the Left Party politician did indeed consider herself antisemitic. 

Not only that, the suit stated, Dobrindt's remark would "undermine her integrity as a political officeholder" and hinder her attempts to form a government in Berlin.

It was not the first time the Left Party has got its lawyers involved following its election victory, as it gets bombarded by accusations of antisemitism from the center right, especially over an incident at an election campaign event in Berlin when a rapper chanted "Death to the IDF" — the Israel Defense Forces, or the Israeli army.

Economy Minister Katherina Reiche also angered the socialist party by giving a speech in which she said that the party was now "openly embracing antisemitism." A video of the speech was posted on the Economy Ministry's Instagram account.

Power of the lawsuit

The lawsuit has become an increasingly popular weapon in German politics in recent years, usually by deploying sections 185, 186 and 187 of the German Criminal Code, which cover offenses including insult, defamation and "intentional defamation," which means knowingly asserting or disseminating untrue facts about others. Theoretically, the punishment can be a fine or up to a year in prison.

In September 2025, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) pressed defamation charges against ChancellorFriedrich Merz after he said that the far-right party's policy of remigration amounted to "ethnic cleansing." 

Similarly, the Green Party in Berlin brought hate speech charges against Merz last year, when he said "we still have this problem in the cityscape" when describing the presence of immigrants.

In another case, the Green Party's own Robert Habeck was sued in 2024 by the Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason(BSW) for claiming that the new upstart party was "buying votes" on the internet by building up "troll armies." Prosecutors dropped the case after Habeck agreed to pay €12,000 ($13,500) to three charities without admitting any wrongdoing, on the grounds that there was only limited public interest in a criminal procedure. 

But charges like these, especially when politicians claim defamation, have little chance of success. "Prosecutors usually dismiss such cases very quickly due to a lack of sufficient grounds for suspicion," media lawyer Christian Solmecke, of the firm WBS Legal, told DW in an email.

"The Federal Constitutional Court has consistently held that, in the political arena, the boundaries of what is permissible are significantly wider than in the private sphere," Solmecke added. "Anyone who voluntarily enters the political arena must also be prepared to endure sharp, polemical, exaggerated and hurtful criticism."

Felix Zimmermann, editor-in-chief of the legal affairs outletLegal Tribune Online (LTO), agrees, because German law makes a careful distinction between an opinion and a false statement. "'Antisemitic' or 'not antisemitic' is an opinion, especially at the moment, when people have very different definitions of it," Zimmermann told DW.

Lawsuits as PR

That hasn't deterred politicians from trying it more and more often. "We are undoubtedly observing a new level of intensity and scale of this practice," said Solmecke. "Political culture has become harsher and more polarized. The threshold for no longer merely engaging political opponents through debate, but instead outright criminalizing them, has dropped dramatically."

The danger, Solmecke argues, is that this often amounts to the "misuse" of law enforcement agencies as political instruments.

But lawfare appears to be effective as a political tactic, not least because it's a guaranteed headline. "From the point of view of the parties filing the complaints, they are highly effective as a PR strategy," said Solmecke. "The political benefit arises entirely independently of the legal outcome."

In the Left Party's case, Zimmermann thinks it certainly pays to show you won't stand to be called antisemitic — not least because Eralp has repeatedly underlined her commitment to the Jewish community in Berlin.

"I think it's mainly about the fact that the Left Party wants to form a coalition in Berlin and Ms. Eralp wants to become mayor," Zimmermann said. "So of course it's good if you're insulted to challenge it, as a signal."

When lawsuits have a constitutional point

The motion against Katherina Reiche, on the other hand, may have much better chances — because she chose to post her inflammatory speech on the Economy Ministry's official social media channels. This could, Zimmermann said, well be seen as a violation of the "principle of neutrality," a constitutional rule that forbids the state from vilifying any particular political party.

"That is of course difficult for a politician, because if they say it on their own account they're allowed, but if they say it on the ministry's account they're not allowed," said Zimmermann. "It's a little absurd, because you're effectively splitting one person into two."

But even though the Left Party filed the complaint against Reiche as an urgent motion, the Constitutional Court may take several weeks, if not months, to actually decide the case — by which time the coalition negotiations in Berlin may have long since finished and Reiche's speech has had its effect. 

The consequences for Reiche, in other words, will be limited — even if her ministry is forced to take down the post and the Left Party can eventually claim a victory.

Edited by: Rina Goldenberg

entries.title: Trump claims Russia and Ukraine agreed to 'energy ceasefire'
entries.summary: US President Donald Trump says both sides have agreed to stop targeting oil refineries, power plants and other energy infrastructure immediately.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Trump says Russia, Ukraine agree to 'energy ceasefire'

October 11, 2026

US President Donald Trump says both sides have agreed to stop targeting oil refineries, power plants and other energy infrastructure immediately.

US President Donald Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to halt strikes on each other's energy infrastructure.

"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine," the president wrote on his Truth Social network.

Trump continued: "Both parties have agreed," before urging restraint from both Kyiv and Moscow: "Do not break it!"

Zelenskyy: Energy ceasefire 'news for me'

There was ‌no immediate ​confirmation ⁠from Moscow, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the news site Axios within minutes of Trump's post that the ceasefire was "news for me."

"The ceasefire announcement was news for me. But if Russians agree to an energy ceasefire, Ukraine will agree. If President Trump negotiated it with Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins; we are ready and we will accept it," he told Axios.

In a social media post later, Zelenskyy said a drone had hit a Kyiv power plant, leading to power outages in the capital.

The Ukrainian leader had earlier repeated his stance that Ukraine would stop hitting Russian oil refineries if the Kremlin curbed its energy attacks.

Trump and Zelenskyy have argued this week over Ukraine's attacks on Russian diesel facilities, which the US president said have contributed to a global diesel shortage, rather than the Iran war.

Trump needs lower fuel prices before midterms

Trump said Friday he had struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia.

The controversial move was an attempt to bring down high fuel prices ahead of the US midterm elections next month.

However, this move undercuts fresh US sanctions Trump signed just weeks ago to further hurt Russian energy revenues funding the war.

On Sunday, a bipartisan group fo six US senators called on the Trump administarion to "immediately reverse course" and scrap the diesel deal.

The signatories included Democrats Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire and Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, and Republicans Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah.

"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the senators said in a joint statement.

European leaders rally behind Zelenskyy

Backing Zelenskyy in the Trump row, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said that she "fully supported" the call for a "ceasefire that protects global food supplies and energy infrastructure in Ukraine and Russia."

"And my full support for President Zelenskyy as he leads the fight for his people's freedom," she wrote online.

On X, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said his country "strongly supports" Trump's call for a "sustained energy ceasefire to start now," which he said Kyiv was ready to honor "if Russia stops its attacks."

French President Emmanuel Macron said his country backs a "real energy ceasefire," but lamented that "Russia continues to refuse that."

After earlier denouncing the Trump-Putin deal, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he supported the energy ceasefire, in a phone call with Trump, his office said.

Blackouts and refinery strikes

Russia has repeatedly struck Ukraine's power plants and transmission lines around Kyiv, Kharkiv, Odesa and elsewhere, to lower civilian morale, especially during the winter months.

Recently, Ukraine has stepped up long-range strikes deep inside Russian territory, targeting major oil refineries and other facilities to curb Moscow's refining capacity and fuel supplies.

Kyiv on Sunday pressed on its campaign against Russian infrastructure, hitting a data center run by Russian technology giant Yandex.

It was the third strike on the company’s facilities in four days.

Edited by: Srinivas Mazumdaru

entries.title: Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove lump on lung
entries.summary: The pontiff said he would be operated on "in the coming days" to remove a lung nodule, which he said was found at "a very early stage."
entries.content:
Vatican

Pope Leo XIV to undergo surgery to remove lump on lung

October 11, 2026

The pontiff said he would be operated on "in the coming days" to remove a lung nodule, which he said was found at "a very early stage."

Pope Leo XIV said Sunday that he will undergo surgery this week to remove a lump on his lung.

"During recent medical checks, a nodule on my lung was found. It has been detected at a very early stage and is very localized," the 71-year-old said during his weekly address in St Peter's Square in the Vatican.

"The doctors believe it would be right to intervene and so, following their advice, I have decided to have the operation to remove it. The operation is already planned in the coming days," he added.

What do we know about the pope's condition?

This is his first major health scare since the 71-year-old American became pope in 2025.

A lung nodule is a small, contained lesion that is smaller than 3 centimeters (1 inch) and can be benign.

According to the American Thoracic Society, fewer than 5% of lung nodules turn out to be cancerous.

The American Cancer Society says the nodules sometimes appear on CT scans of the chest or abdomen during searches for trauma or lung infections that are unrelated to cancer screenings.

Leo is younger than most popes. His predecessor, Francis, was five years older when he assumed the role, while Francis' predecessor, Benedict XVI, was 78 at the start of his tenure.

Leo is not known to have had any previous health issues, and leads a relatively active lifestyle.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

entries.title: A migrant boat sank off the coast of Djibouti with the UN reporting over 200 people dead or missing
entries.summary: The UN migration agency has reported that at least 139 people were killed and 84 remain missing after a migrant boat sank overnight on its way to Yemen. At least 80 Ethiopians survived the incident but 15 children died.
entries.content:
October 11, 2026

The UN migration agency has reported that at least 139 people were killed and 84 remain missing after a migrant boat sank overnight on its way to Yemen. At least 80 Ethiopians survived the incident but 15 children died.

The United Nations International Organization for Migration (IOM) on Sunday said that at least 139 people were killed when a migrant boat carrying an estimated 305 people capsized off the coast of Djibouti in northeastern Africa.

At least 84 people remained missing in what is thought to be one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.

In a statement, IOM Chief of Mission in Djibouti Alexandre Coissac called the loss of life "devastating," adding, "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities" by trying to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and reach Gulf countries.

"Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East," according to the IOM.

IOM representatives said, "Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing."

Djibouti to Yemen a dangerous crossing

The IOM says it has detected more than 20,000 crossings from Djibouti to Yemen — which is currently in the middle of a raging civil war — in the past month. More than 900 migrants were killed attempting the passage in 2025.

The IOM says most of those attempting to cross are from Ethiopia and Somalia. The 80 survivors from Saturday night's capsizing were all Ethiopian nationals.

The IOM on Sunday urged "donors and partners to strengthen support for Djibouti's response, including search and rescue operations and life-saving assistance."

Of the bodies so far recovered, 52 were men, 42 were women and 15 were children.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn
